say: You give it a calculation. It gives back a quick **estimate**, close to the real answer, that you can do in your head.
The key idea: round every number to one **significant figure** first. Then the sum is easy, and the answer shows if your calculator work is sensible.

how.ordinary: Ordinary level uses it as a short part on Paper 2, for example estimating a height or a number of times, worth 5 marks, and as a check inside longer measurement questions.

example.question:
A shop sells $19.8$ kg of cheese at $€6.10$ per kg.
(a) Estimate the cost by rounding each number to one significant figure.
(b) Calculate the exact cost.
(c) Is your answer to (b) sensible?

steps.title: Round each number
steps.say: Round each number to one significant figure. Keep the first digit that is not zero and round the rest.

steps.title: Multiply the rounded numbers
steps.say: Now multiply the easy numbers. This is the **estimate**.

steps.title: Calculate exactly
steps.say: Use the original numbers. Multiply the weight by the price per kg.

steps.title: Compare the two
steps.say: Put the exact answer next to the estimate. They should be close.

lines.text: The difference is under €1. The exact cost of $\hl{2}{€120.78}$ is sensible.

ordinary.tip: Show the working for your estimate. A wrong box ticked or a slightly wrong estimate still earns marks if your working is consistent with it.

say: You give it a cost price and a selling price. It finds the **profit**, the **mark-up** and the **margin**.
The key idea: profit is selling price minus cost price. Mark-up is that profit as a percentage of the **cost price**. Margin is the same profit as a percentage of the **selling price**.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as a step inside Paper 1 money questions, for example turning a margin of 18% into a mark-up of 22% (5 marks), or comparing two ways to write a percentage of a price (10 marks).
how.ordinary: Ordinary level uses it in Paper 1 Question 6, where a mark-up gives a selling price and then the profit is found as a percentage of that selling price (10 marks).

example.question: A shop buys a bag for $€45$ and sells it for $€60$. Find (a) the profit, (b) the mark-up as a percentage of the cost price, (c) the margin as a percentage of the selling price.

steps.title: Find the profit
steps.say: Profit is the selling price minus the cost price.

steps.title: Find the mark-up
steps.say: Mark-up divides the profit by the cost price. The cost price is the one the shop paid.

steps.title: Find the margin
steps.say: Margin divides the same profit by the selling price instead.

steps.title: Check the two
steps.say: The profit is the same in both. Only the number you divide by changes.

lines.text: Mark-up divides by $45$, the cost. Margin divides by $60$, the selling price.

higher.tip: When a question gives a margin, write the cost price as a percentage of the selling price first. That earns credit before any mark-up is found.
Do not test the answer with numbers you pick. Write each option using the letters in the question, because checking one set of values earns at most low partial credit.

sources.quote: is given at most Low Partial Credit

ordinary.tip: If the question gives an answer without work, you can still get full marks for the first part, but show your work anyway so a slip does not lose the rest.

sources.quote: Accept correct answer without work for (i)

ordinary.tip: In the second part, use your answer from the first. Using it is work of merit even when it is not fully correct.

say: You give it a starting amount $P$, a yearly rate and a number of years. It gives back the **final value** $F$.
The key idea: each year the amount is multiplied by the same number, $1 + i$. So after $t$ years you multiply $t$ times, which is $F = P(1 + i)^t$.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as the first part of a Paper 1 money question (5 marks, for example $F = 3000(1 + 0.024)^3$), and then builds on it with present value and rates.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it in Paper 1 almost every year, as a 5 or 10 mark part: the final value, the starting amount worked backwards, or the rate.

example.question: Aoife invests $€7000$ at $2.5\%$ per year compound interest for $3$ years. Find the value of her investment at the end of $3$ years, to the nearest cent.

steps.title: Write the formula
steps.say: Each year the amount grows by the rate. Write the formula for $t$ years.

steps.title: Write down what you know
steps.say: Change $2.5\%$ to a decimal. Then list the three values.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.say: Put the numbers into the formula. Add $1$ to $\hl{1}{i}$ first.

steps.title: Calculate
steps.say: Work out the power, then multiply. Round to the cent at the end.

higher.tip: Even a part-way answer earns marks: change the rate to a decimal, or substitute into the formula.
Give a rate as a percentage. Leaving it as a decimal loses a mark.

ordinary.tip: Write the formula out with every number substituted. Fully substituted earns high partial credit even if you do not finish.
Writing the correct formula on its own earns marks, so start with it.
The list method works too. Finding the amount year by year, with the correct amounts for most years, earns high partial credit.
For a part with only a short answer, it can be accepted without work, but a wrong answer with no work earns nothing. Show the calculation.

sources.quote: Accept correct answer without work for (i)

say: You give it a starting value $P$, a yearly rate of loss and a number of years. It gives back the **value** $F$ after those years.
The key idea: each year the value is multiplied by the same number, $1 - i$, because the car keeps $100\% - i$ of what it was worth. So $F = P(1 - i)^t$.

how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it on Paper 1 in most years, as a 5 or 10 mark part: the value of a car after some years, often followed by a graph or a percentage loss.

example.question: A van costs $€25\,000$ new. It loses $10\%$ of its value each year. Find the value of the van after $4$ years.

steps.title: Find the yearly multiplier
steps.say: The van keeps $90\%$ of its value each year. Write that as a decimal.

steps.title: Write the formula
steps.say: Each year the value is multiplied by $\hl{2}{0.9}$. After $t$ years that is $t$ times.

ordinary.tip: Write the depreciation formula down first. A correct formula on its own earns marks.
In a formula you make up yourself, three things must be right: the starting value, the multiplier, and the power. Two correct earns high partial credit.
Writing $t$ down is marked as work of merit. Say how many years the question asks for.
Year by year works as a second method. List each year's value and keep going to the year asked for.
